en: To make a bad situation better
hook: AMELIORATE: 'meliorate' sounds like 'better' (meilleur in French). Make better.
story: Ameliorate. To make a bad situation better. Every afternoon, the road outside Tasfia's school in Mirpur turned into chaos: rickshaws, cars and children all tangled together in the heat. Then a group of parents began volunteering as crossing guards, and the school moved its closing time by fifteen minutes. The jam did not vanish, but the changes ameliorated it a great deal. Ameliorate comes from the Latin melior, meaning better, as in the French meilleur: to ameliorate is to make better. So, what verb means to improve a bad situation? ... Ameliorate.

gre.s: The new irrigation canals did much to ____ the effects of the drought, though they could not entirely prevent crop losses.
gre.clue: though they could not entirely prevent crop losses

example: Planting trees along the busy roads of Gazipur could ameliorate the summer heat for thousands of factory workers.

en: To cause someone to become hostile or annoyed
bn: বিরূপ করে তোলা; শত্রুতা সৃষ্টি করা
hook: ANTAGONIZE: turn someone into your ANTAGONIST (enemy).
story: Antagonize. To cause someone to become hostile or annoyed. Rumon wanted his landlord to fix the water pump. Instead of asking politely, he sent angry messages at midnight and complained loudly on the stairs. The landlord, who had always been friendly, now refused even to answer. [sigh] Rumon had antagonized the one person who could help him. In the end, his wife fixed things with a polite visit and a box of sweets. To antagonize someone is to turn them into your antagonist, the villain against you. So, what verb means to make someone hostile toward you? ... Antagonize.

gre.s: Eager not to ____ the powerful landlords whose support he needed, the reformer softened his proposals until they offended no one.
gre.clue: until they offended no one

example: The referee's arrogant manner antagonized both teams, and by halftime even the home fans were jeering him.

en: The highest or most successful point; the point in an orbit farthest from Earth
hook: APO-GEE: AWAY (apo) from Earth (geo), the farthest, highest point.
story: Apogee. The highest or most successful point; also, the point in an orbit farthest from Earth. Nabila's grandfather played football in Dhaka in the nineteen seventies. The apogee of his career came when he scored the winning goal in a derby before a packed stadium; he still keeps the yellowed newspaper clipping. In science class, Nabila learned the other meaning: the moon's apogee is where it swings farthest from Earth. Apo means away, and gee comes from the Greek for Earth, as in geography. So, what word means the high point, or the farthest point of an orbit? ... Apogee.

gre.s: Critics agree that the novelist's career reached its ____ with her third book; nothing she wrote afterward came close to its brilliance or its success.
gre.clue: nothing she wrote afterward came close

example: Many scholars regard the reign of Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, as the apogee of Mughal architecture.

en: Humorously rude and indecent
hook: BAWDY: BAWLING out rude jokes.
story: Bawdy. Humorously rude and indecent. At a village jatra performance, a clown came on between the serious scenes and told bawdy jokes about husbands, wives and a runaway lungi. The men at the back roared, the aunties covered their mouths, and Hafiz's grandmother [chuckle] pretended not to hear, though her shoulders were shaking. The jokes were rude, but in a cheerful, old-fashioned way. Bawdy sounds like rowdy, and bawdy humour is rowdy and rude. So, what word describes humour that is rude but merry? ... Bawdy.

gre.s: The comedian's ____ jokes, full of sexual innuendo, delighted the late-night crowd but would never have been permitted on family television.
gre.clue: full of sexual innuendo

example: Chaucer's bawdy tales of millers and cheating wives still make university students blush and laugh.

en: A large, destructive fire
hook: CONFLAGRATION: a FLAG-burning FLAME everywhere.
story: Conflagration. A large, destructive fire. One night in old Dhaka, a fire that began in a building storing chemicals spread through the narrow lanes of Chawkbazar. Within minutes, buildings, cars and shops were burning, and the flames turned the sky orange. Juthi watched from a distant rooftop, her hands pressed to her mouth. Firefighters fought the conflagration until dawn. Conflagration comes from the Latin flagrare, to burn, the same root as flagrant, which once meant blazing. So, what word means a huge, destructive fire? ... Conflagration.

gre.s: What began as a small kitchen fire soon became a ____ that consumed half the town, as dry winds drove the flames from roof to roof.
gre.clue: consumed half the town

example: The Great Fire of London in 1666 was a conflagration that destroyed more than thirteen thousand houses.

en: Pleasant and friendly; well suited to one's taste or nature
hook: CON-GENIAL: comes with a GENIAL, friendly feeling.
story: Congenial. Pleasant and friendly; well suited to one's taste or nature. When Raihan moved to Sylhet for his first job, he worried about living with strangers. But his new flatmates were congenial: they shared their tea, invited him on weekend trips to the tea gardens, and laughed at his terrible jokes. [laugh] The quiet green town was congenial to him too, after the noise of Dhaka. Congenial contains genial, which means warm and friendly. So, what word describes people or a place that suits you and makes you feel at home? ... Congenial.

gre.s: Although the two scientists had been bitter rivals in print, they found each other surprisingly ____ in person, chatting amiably for hours.
gre.clue: chatting amiably for hours

example: Rahim found the quiet public library in Chattogram far more congenial for study than his family's noisy flat.

en: To describe or portray precisely; to mark the boundary of
bn: সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে বর্ণনা করা; সীমা নির্ধারণ করা
hook: DE-LINE-ATE: draw the LINES clearly.
story: Delineate. To describe or portray precisely; to mark the boundary of. When two brothers in Mukit's village disagreed about where their land ended, a government surveyor arrived with a long measuring chain and an old map. He walked the field all afternoon and drove bamboo stakes into the mud to delineate the boundary. Then he delineated his reasons in a clear report that both brothers signed. Delineate contains line: to delineate is to draw the lines clearly. So, what verb means to mark out or describe something precisely? ... Delineate.

gre.s: Because the old treaty failed to ____ the border precisely, both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank.
gre.clue: both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank

example: The new contract clearly delineates who must pay for repairs, ending years of argument between the tenants and the owner.

en: To criticize unfairly; to belittle
hook: DENIGRATE: blacken (niger) someone's name.
story: Denigrate. To criticize unfairly; to belittle. Whenever Afsana talked about studying fashion design, her uncle denigrated the idea. "Sewing is not a career," he said, "it is a hobby." He called her sketches childish in front of the family. Afsana kept drawing anyway. Five years later, her uncle wore a panjabi she had designed to a wedding, [chuckle] and he praised it all evening. Denigrate comes from the Latin for to blacken: to denigrate someone is to blacken their name or their work. So, what verb means to unfairly belittle someone? ... Denigrate.

gre.s: Rather than engage with the substance of her argument, her rivals chose to ____ her credentials, dismissing her as a mere amateur despite her decades of research.
gre.clue: dismissing her as a mere amateur

example: Some nineteenth-century critics denigrated photography as a mechanical trick, unworthy of being called an art.

en: Holding total power and often using it cruelly
hook: DESPOTIC: a DESPOT, an all-powerful tyrant.
story: Despotic. Holding total power and often using it cruelly. In history class, Ishraq read about despotic kings who could jail anyone for a single word of criticism, and whose subjects whispered even at home. That night he remembered the headmaster of his old school, who had banned talking in the corridors and punished boys for the wrong colour of socks. Even that small despotic rule had made the children miserable. A despot is an all-powerful ruler, and despotic describes the way a despot rules. So, what word describes a ruler with total, cruel power? ... Despotic.

gre.s: The new leader, who had promised a return to democracy, soon proved just as ____ as his predecessor, jailing critics and ruling by decree.
gre.clue: jailing critics and ruling by decree

example: Under the despotic governor, newspapers were shut down and any farmer who complained about taxes risked prison.

en: A long, angry speech or piece of writing attacking someone
hook: DIATRIBE: a speech that would make a whole TRIBE DIE of embarrassment.
story: Diatribe. A long, angry speech or piece of writing attacking someone. When the internet went off in the middle of the cricket final, Maisha's father called the helpline and delivered a diatribe that lasted twenty minutes. He attacked the company, its manager, its prices and even its music on hold. At last the operator said quietly, "Sir, your bill was not paid." The diatribe ended at once. Hear tribe inside diatribe: picture someone shouting angrily at a whole tribe for an hour. So, what word means a long, bitter verbal attack? ... Diatribe.

gre.s: What began as a measured critique of the policy soon devolved into a ____ against everyone who had ever supported it.
gre.clue: What began as a measured critique

example: The retired colonel's letter to the editor was a diatribe against cyclists, whom he blamed for every traffic jam in town.

en: Amusing in a dry, odd, or whimsical way
hook: DROLL: a DOLL that makes funny, dry jokes.
story: Droll. Amusing in a dry, odd, or whimsical way. Shafin's grandfather never laughed at his own jokes. When the electricity went out during a storm, he lit a candle and said, without smiling, "Ah, at last, a romantic dinner, courtesy of the power company." [laugh] Everyone burst out laughing, but his face stayed perfectly straight. His humour was always droll. Droll comes from the French drôle, meaning funny, and droll humour is quiet, dry and a little odd. So, what word describes dry, quirky humour? ... Droll.

gre.s: The memoir's ____ observations, delivered with a perfectly straight face, had readers laughing at the most mundane details of office life.
gre.clue: had readers laughing

example: The museum guide had a droll way of describing ancient tax collectors that kept the bored students giggling.

en: To fill with delight; to charm
hook: EN-CHANT: like a magical CHANT that casts a spell.
story: Enchant. To fill with delight; to charm. On her first visit to Ratargul, the freshwater swamp forest near Sylhet, Ratna sat in a small wooden boat as it slid between trees standing in green water. Birds called overhead, and sunlight fell in pieces on the surface. [gasp] She had never seen anything so lovely. The forest enchanted her completely. Enchant contains chant, like a magic song that casts a spell: when something enchants you, you are under its spell. So, what verb means to fill someone with delight, as if by magic? ... Enchant.

gre.s: The village's winding lanes and flower-covered cottages never fail to ____ visitors, many of whom return year after year.
gre.clue: many of whom return year after year

example: The puppet show at Shilpakala Academy enchanted the children, who sat in complete silence for an hour.

en: To keep away from something on purpose
hook: ESCHEW: sounds like a sneeze, 'ah-CHOO!' — you avoid it.
story: Eschew. To keep away from something on purpose. After his father's heart attack, Fuad decided to change his own habits. He began to eschew sugar in his tea, fried snacks at the office, and late nights on his phone. At first it was hard to refuse his colleagues' samosas, but within a few months he felt lighter and stronger. Eschew sounds like a sneeze, ah choo: you turn away from a sneeze, and you eschew whatever you choose to avoid. So, what verb means to deliberately avoid something? ... Eschew.

gre.s: The minimalist architect tended to ____ ornament of any kind, preferring bare concrete and plain glass.
gre.clue: preferring bare concrete and plain glass

example: The young poet eschewed rhyme altogether, believing it made her verses sound like advertising jingles.

en: To pretend to be affected by a feeling or state
hook: FEIGN: sounds like FAKE + FAINT; fake a faint.
story: Feign. To pretend to be affected by a feeling or state. On the morning of her maths test, Sinthia lay in bed clutching her stomach and moaning softly. She was feigning illness. Her mother felt her forehead, found it cool, and said, "Then you will not want your favourite paratha for breakfast." Sinthia sat up at once. [chuckle] Her feigned pain had vanished. Feign shares its Latin root with fiction: both mean to make something up. So, what verb means to pretend to feel something? ... Feign.

gre.s: Though secretly delighted by the news, the diplomat chose to ____ indifference so as not to reveal his government's hand.
gre.clue: so as not to reveal his government's hand

example: Mahin feigned surprise when his friends burst in with a cake, though he had overheard their plans a week earlier.

en: Recklessly bold or rash
hook: FOOL-HARDY: a FOOL who's too HARDY for his own good.
story: Foolhardy. Recklessly bold or rash. Every monsoon, the news shows young men riding on the roofs of crowded trains, or taking selfies at the edge of rushing waterfalls. Ayan's cousin once tried to swim across the swollen Karnaphuli river on a bet, and a fishing boat had to pull him out. His mother called it the most foolhardy thing he had ever done. Hardy means bold and tough, so foolhardy is the boldness of a fool. So, what word describes someone recklessly daring? ... Foolhardy.

gre.s: Experienced mountaineers considered the attempt ____, since the climbers planned to ascend in midwinter without oxygen or guides.
gre.clue: in midwinter without oxygen or guides

example: Selling the family shop to buy cryptocurrency on a stranger's tip was a foolhardy move that Kamal deeply regretted.

en: Acting suddenly, on impulse, without thinking first
hook: IMPETUOUS: full of IMPETUS (sudden force), no brakes.
story: Impetuous. Acting suddenly, on impulse, without thinking first. Walking through the pet market at Katabon, Nusaiba fell in love with a parrot that could say hello. Without asking her parents or her landlord, she bought it, a cage and a bag of seeds on the spot. That night the parrot screeched until dawn, and the landlord knocked on her door. It had been an impetuous purchase. Impetuous comes from impetus, a sudden force that pushes forward with no brakes. So, what word describes someone who acts on sudden impulse? ... Impetuous.

gre.s: The general's ____ decision to attack before reinforcements arrived, made in a moment of anger, cost him the battle.
gre.clue: made in a moment of anger

example: In an impetuous moment, the young batsman charged down the pitch to the very first ball and was stumped.

en: Seemingly endless; tediously long
hook: IN-TERMINABLE: can't be TERMINATED.
story: Interminable. Seemingly endless; tediously long. Habib's flight from Dhaka to Toronto had a twelve-hour stopover in a quiet airport. He walked every corridor, read every sign, and drank four cups of bad coffee, but the clock barely moved. The wait felt interminable. Then the second flight was delayed, and the interminable day grew even longer. In means not, and terminate means to end: interminable describes something that seems to have no end. So, what word describes a wait that seems to go on forever? ... Interminable.

gre.s: Audiences who had expected a brisk thriller found the film ____: its three-hour running time was padded with lengthy scenes in which almost nothing happened.
gre.clue: padded with lengthy scenes in which almost nothing happened

example: Stuck in an interminable traffic jam on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, Shirin finished an entire novel.

en: A joking attitude toward something that deserves seriousness
hook: LEVITY: LIGHT as LEVITATING.
story: Levity. A joking attitude toward something that deserves seriousness. At the hospital where Lubna's father was having surgery, the family waited in silence. Then her young cousin began making jokes about the hospital food and the doctor's moustache. Her aunt gave him a sharp look. This was not the time for levity. Later, when the surgery went well, a little levity was finally welcome. Levity comes from the Latin levis, light, as in levitate: levity treats heavy things too lightly. So, what word means inappropriate lightness about something serious? ... Levity.

gre.s: The speaker's ____ seemed badly misjudged; his jokes about the earthquake offended an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims.
gre.clue: an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims

example: The judge warned that any further levity in the courtroom would be treated as contempt.

en: Illegal or dishonest acts by someone in an official post
hook: MAL-FEASANCE: BAD doing (mal = bad).
story: Malfeasance. Illegal or dishonest acts by someone in an official post. A government engineer in Rajib's district approved a new school building made with half the steel the design required, and quietly pocketed the rest of the money. When cracks appeared within a year, investigators traced the paperwork back to him. He was charged with malfeasance and dismissed. Mal means bad, as in malpractice, and feasance comes from the French for doing: malfeasance is bad doing by an official. So, what word means wrongdoing by a public official? ... Malfeasance.

gre.s: Once celebrated as a reformer, the mayor left office in disgrace after an inquiry uncovered years of ____, including bribery and the theft of public funds.
gre.clue: including bribery and the theft of public funds

example: Investigators found evidence of malfeasance at the port authority, where officials had been taking bribes to release cargo uninspected.

en: To speak harmful untruths about someone (verb); evil or harmful (adjective)
hook: MAL = bad. To say bad things about someone.
story: Malign. As a verb, to speak harmful untruths about someone. As an adjective, evil or harmful. When Tamim opened a small bakery that quickly became popular, a rival shop owner began to malign him, telling customers that Tamim used stale flour and dirty water. None of it was true. Tamim invited everyone to watch him bake in his open kitchen, and the rumours died. Those who malign others often reveal their own malign intentions. Mal means bad: to malign someone is to speak badly of them. So, what verb means to spread harmful lies about someone? ... Malign.

gre.s: Although tabloids continue to ____ the senator as corrupt, every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper.
gre.clue: every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper

example: Anonymous accounts maligned the young cricketer online, falsely claiming that he had taken money to lose matches.

en: Former
hook: ONETIME: ONE TIME in the past.
story: Onetime. Former. In a small tea shop in Narail, Mehnaz met an old man who quietly mentioned that he was a onetime member of the national football team. Now he sells tea and biscuits, and few customers know his past. He showed her a faded photograph from his playing days, and his eyes shone. Do not confuse onetime with a one-time event that happens only once; a onetime champion was a champion once, in the past. So, what word means former, as in someone who once held a role? ... Onetime.

gre.s: The senator, a ____ ally of the president, has become one of his fiercest critics since their bitter public quarrel over the budget last year.
gre.clue: has become one of his fiercest critics

example: Sabina, a onetime nurse, now runs a small bakery in Uttara that is famous for its mango cakes.

en: A person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts
hook: PHILISTINE: thinks a museum is a waste of land.
story: Philistine. A person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts. When the old art college building in Khaled's town was set to be demolished for a car park, one businessman laughed. "Paintings do not feed anyone," he said. "Give me parking." Khaled, an art student, felt hurt. To him the man was a philistine, blind to everything beautiful the building had nurtured. In the Bible, the Philistines were enemies of the Israelites, and nineteenth-century writers borrowed the name for people who scorn culture. So, what word describes someone who has no time for art? ... Philistine.

gre.s: Dismissing the museum as a waste of public money, the mayor revealed himself to be a ____, indifferent to the paintings and sculptures that had made the city famous.
gre.clue: indifferent to the paintings and sculptures

example: Only a philistine would cover the wall of a centuries-old terracotta temple with advertising posters.

en: Slow, heavy, and monotonous; working steadily but without inspiration
hook: PLODDING: the PLOD-PLOD sound of tired, heavy footsteps.
story: Plodding. Slow, heavy, and monotonous; working steadily but without inspiration. Proma's history textbook was plodding: page after page of dates and names, with no stories and no pictures. She fell asleep over it every night. Her classmate's plodding effort, though, paid off; he read slowly, ten pages a day, and never missed one. Plod is the sound of tired, heavy footsteps, plod, plod, plod, and plodding work moves at that same heavy pace. So, what word describes something slow, steady and dull? ... Plodding.

gre.s: Critics praised the film's acting but found its ____ pace exhausting, as scenes dragged on long after their point had been made.
gre.clue: scenes dragged on long after their point had been made

example: The biography's plodding chapters on tax records nearly made me give up before reaching the exciting war years.

en: Dangerously steep; sudden and dramatic
hook: PRECIPITOUS: like a PRECIPICE, a sheer cliff.
story: Precipitous. Dangerously steep; sudden and dramatic. On a trek to Keokradong in Bandarban, Sabina reached a narrow path along a precipitous slope, with a sheer drop to the jungle below. [gasp] She pressed her back to the rock and inched forward. That same month, the price of tomatoes made a precipitous fall after a bumper harvest. Precipitous is linked to precipice, a sheer cliff; do not confuse it with precipitate, which describes a rash action. So, what word describes a slope or drop that is dangerously steep? ... Precipitous.

gre.s: The company's decline was ____: in a single quarter, its share price fell by ninety percent, wiping out a decade of steady growth.
gre.clue: in a single quarter

example: After the mill closed, the town's population suffered a precipitous fall, from forty thousand to barely ten thousand.

en: Ordinary and dull; lacking imagination
hook: PROSAIC: like plain PROSE, not poetry.
story: Prosaic. Ordinary and dull; lacking imagination. Turjo asked his grandfather how he had met his grandmother, hoping for a love story full of monsoon rain and poetry. "We met at the post office," his grandfather said. "She was in the queue before me." That was all. [chuckle] It was a prosaic answer, but his grandmother smiled across the room as if it were the most beautiful story in the world. Prosaic comes from prose, plain writing rather than poetry. So, what word describes something ordinary and unpoetic? ... Prosaic.

gre.s: Fans expecting a dramatic explanation for the band's breakup were disappointed by the ____ truth: the members had simply grown tired of touring.
gre.clue: had simply grown tired of touring

example: The famous painter's daily routine turned out to be prosaic, with breakfast at seven, work until noon, and an afternoon nap.

en: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
hook: QUANDARY: 'QUAND?' (when?) and 'where?' — totally stuck.
story: Quandary. A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation. Shefali received two offers on the same day: a scholarship to study in Japan, and a good job in Dhaka near her ageing parents. Taking one meant losing the other. For a week she barely slept. She was in a real quandary. Finally, her mother told her to go, and promised to call every night. Quandary sounds like wander, and in a quandary your mind wanders back and forth, unable to choose. So, what word means being stuck between difficult choices? ... Quandary.

gre.s: The doctor faced a genuine ____: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate her duty of honesty.
gre.clue: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate

example: The referee faced a quandary when the floodlights failed with the scores level and only two minutes left to play.

en: To damage or destroy something badly over a wide area
hook: RAVAGE: like a RAVENOUS SAVAGE destroying everything.
story: Ravage. To damage or destroy something badly over a wide area. In the spring of two thousand seventeen, flash floods ravaged the haor wetlands of Sunamganj. In a few days the water swallowed most of the rice harvest, months of work gone. Adnan's uncle stood at the edge of his field and saw only grey water where golden paddy had been. Ravage sounds like savage: ravaging forces destroy savagely and widely. So, what verb means to cause widespread destruction? ... Ravage.

gre.s: Unless farmers act quickly to control the locusts, the swarms will ____ the region's crops, leaving little to harvest and threatening famine.
gre.clue: leaving little to harvest

example: Years of civil war had ravaged the country's roads, so aid trucks needed four days to cover two hundred kilometres.

en: Making a show of being morally superior to others
hook: SANCTIMONIOUS: acts like a SAINT, but it's all for MONEY and show.
story: Sanctimonious. Making a show of being morally superior to others. At a family gathering, Rokshana's uncle lectured everyone about honesty, saying young people today had no morals. He spoke loudly so the neighbours could hear. Rokshana knew that the same uncle had cheated his own brother out of a plot of land. His sanctimonious speech made her feel sick. Sanct means holy, as in sanctuary and saint: a sanctimonious person puts on a show of holiness. So, what word describes someone smugly preaching about their own goodness? ... Sanctimonious.

gre.s: Voters grew tired of the senator's ____ speeches about honesty, particularly after he was caught concealing his own debts.
gre.clue: after he was caught concealing his own debts

example: My cousin's sanctimonious posts about healthy eating would be easier to bear if he did not eat fuchka every evening.

en: Very careful to do what is right; extremely attentive to detail
hook: SCRUPULOUS: has SCRUPLES, a moral conscience.
story: Scrupulous. Very careful to do what is right; extremely attentive to detail. When a customer at Iqbal's small grocery shop in Bogura accidentally paid him five hundred taka too much, Iqbal noticed only that evening. He walked two kilometres in the rain to return it. In the shop he is just as scrupulous, weighing every bag of rice twice. A scruple was once a tiny sharp stone, the kind that gets into your sandal; a scrupulous person feels every small wrong, like that stone. So, what word describes someone careful to be honest and exact? ... Scrupulous.

gre.s: The biographer was ____ about sources, refusing to include any anecdote that she could not verify with at least two documents.
gre.clue: refusing to include any anecdote that she could not verify

example: Scrupulous record keeping let the laboratory trace every blood sample back to the exact patient and hour.

en: Serious, respectable, and unadventurous
hook: STAID: STAYED the same forever, never adventurous.
story: Staid. Serious, respectable, and unadventurous. Nafisa's father has worn the same grey trousers to the same bank office for twenty-five years. He eats dinner at nine, reads the same newspaper, and goes to bed at half past ten. So when he announced on his birthday that he wanted a motorbike trip to the hills of Bandarban, [gasp] the family was stunned. Even the most staid man has a spark in him. Staid is an old spelling of stayed: a staid person has always stayed the same. So, what word describes someone serious, steady and never adventurous? ... Staid.

gre.s: Once known for its ____ coverage of parliamentary procedure, the newspaper has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip.
gre.clue: has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip

example: The staid old bank surprised its customers by hiring a rapper to star in its new advertising campaign.
